I often wonder if the NSA managed to seed the GCC and OSS compilers enough in the early days that EVERYTHING from linux to netbsd is backdoored. Theoretically terrifying and possibly true right?

What happens when someone notices their tiny text editing demo program using a network socket they never wrote in, or every single thing they compile from stand alone ELFs to kernel modules ends up with the same chunk of code often at the same offset?

A bad compiler could theoretically make any program do anything it wants but the complexity gets exponentially higher the more you change. Creating a compiler with a local UID trick up its sleeve is one thing, a compiler so pwned it obfuscates its own existence is something else entirely. Which way did that program just perform a memory dump? does the system support a.out or ELF or both? what threads/malloc/string library did they use? The questions and possible answers go on for days. You can't program for everything and once you miss one thing and someone notices its game over.

tl;dr neat thought experiment like schrodinger's cat but not a real thing for practicality and usefulness.

Don't underestimate just how devastatingly effective virtualization makes reverse engineering and forensic analysis. I'm sure the NSA or whoever have the absolute best motherfuckers working on some of the craziest shit in CS. Sure, really old exploits that 'no one' knew about in popular code that goes back YEARS, but there are several key differences. The incentive to keep a discovery secret is much greater in cases of genuine exploits and holes. You get presumed exclusive access. A backdoor on the other hand doesn't have the same level of incentive to keep quiet. You may not be able to utilize it and its implicit that someone put it there and is actively using it besides you. It's also easier to spot live activity from a backdoor than just blended into a flat source code file (random plug http://www.ioccc.org/).
